query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings is primarily due to engineered layering that creates controlled, moderate lattice misfits at the interfaces. These interfacial regions act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and inhibit atomic diffusion, thereby retarding creep deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy coating with a relatively homogeneous single-phase microstructure or minimal interfacial contrast.
generation.intervention: Fabricate and compare multilayer coatings formed by alternating high-entropy alloy layers with slightly differing compositions (and hence lattice parameters) to deliberately introduce controlled interface misfits.
generation.conditions: Under high-temperature and high-stress conditions typical of service environments (e.g., temperatures around 800–1000°C and stresses relevant for protective coatings).
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered multilayer interfaces that possess moderate lattice misfit and corresponding internal stress fields.
generation.mechanism: The lattice misfit at each interface generates local strain fields that impede the nucleation and propagation of dislocations, while also reducing diffusion pathways across layers. This dual barrier effect limits time-dependent plastic (creep) deformation by pinning dislocations at the interlayer boundaries and slowing atomic rearrangements.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a homogeneous (single-layer) high-entropy alloy coating, the multilayer coating will display a significantly reduced steady-state creep rate and accumulate less strain under identical high-temperature, constant-load conditions.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy coatings fabricated without intentional multilayer structuring (i.e., with a uniform, single-phase microstructure).
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be significant under temperatures and stresses that maintain the integrity of the multilayer microstructure. At extreme temperatures or stresses that cause interfacial degradation or phase instability, the effect may diminish.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal lattice misfit range and the relative contributions of dislocation pinning versus diffusion barrier effects are not yet quantitatively defined, and the interplay with other microstructural features (e.g., precipitate distribution) may also affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of high-entropy alloy coatings: one group with engineered multilayer architectures (designed to have controlled lattice misfits at their interfaces) and a control group of homogeneous, single-layer coatings. Subject both groups to identical creep tests at a high temperature (e.g., 900°C) under constant applied stress.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate using strain–time measurements
Total creep strain accumulation over a fixed period
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) focusing on dislocation pinning at interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and lower strain accumulation relative to the homogeneous coatings, or if microstructural analysis does not reveal enhanced dislocation pinning at the interfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 13, all creep curves exhibit the typical three-stage behavior. Notably, the duration of the steady-state creep stage decreases with increasing |δ|. The relationship between creep life and |δ| is non-monotonic. Specifically, within the range of −0.1688% to −0.084%, creep life increases as |δ| increases. Conversely, within the range of −0.8075% to −0.1688%, creep life decreases as |δ| increases. The longest creep life is observed at δ = −0.1688%. To gain further insight into the underlying mechanisms, atomic strain distributions were analyzed, as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14a,b compare atomic strain maps of HESAs with negative (−0.1402%) and positive (0.1402%) lattice misfits. At t = 130 ps, the model with the negative lattice misfit (Figure 14a) exhibits lower atomic strain, suggesting enhanced resistance to deformation. This implies that a negative lattice misfit stabilizes the γ′ phase, strengthens the γ/γ′ interface, and impedes dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility.
